glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 21 opens with the king’s heart in the LORD’s hand and closes with deliverance that belongs to Him, and between those frames it shows a God who weighs hearts and prizes justice above sacrifice, warning against pride, haste, and laziness and commending the righteous man who gives and does not spare.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The sayings continue Solomon’s collection begun at 10:1. Royal and military pictures appear at its beginning, middle, and end (21:1, 22, 31), and paired sayings on worship (21:3, 27) and the contentious woman (21:9, 19) echo across it.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, But the LORD weighs the hearts.” (Proverbs 21:2)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 21 begins on the throne and ends on the battlefield, and both scenes belong to the LORD. “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD” (21:1), and when the horse is ready for war, “deliverance is of the LORD” (21:31). The throne and the army, the two strongest powers in Solomon’s world, both answer to Him.

Inside that frame the chapter keeps returning to what the LORD sees. A man’s way looks right in his own eyes, “But the LORD weighs the hearts” (21:2). Pride is named as sin in “A haughty look, a proud heart” (21:4), and the proud and haughty man bears the name “Scoffer” (21:24). The wicked man “hardens his face” (21:29), but the righteous God “wisely considers the house of the wicked” (21:12) and overthrows them for their wickedness.

The rest weighs what people do with money and need. Treasure won by a lying tongue is a “fleeting fantasy” (21:6), the lover of pleasure ends poor (21:17), and the lazy man is killed by his own desire because his hands refuse to labor (21:25). Against him stands the righteous man who “gives and does not spare” (21:26), alongside the warning that whoever shuts his ears to the poor “Will also cry himself and not be heard” (21:13).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 21:1–3 — The LORD Weighs the Hearts

As a farmer turns water into the channel he chooses, the LORD turns the heart of the most powerful ruler, and He looks past the approval every person gives his own way to weigh the heart itself. What pleases Him more than any sacrifice is a life of righteousness and justice.

Proverbs 21:4–8 — Pride, Haste, and Ill-Gotten Treasure

A haughty look, a proud heart, and even the plowing of the wicked are named together as sin, and the careful plans of the diligent are set against the haste that ends in poverty. Treasure won by lying vanishes like a vapor, the violence of the wicked sweeps them away because they refuse justice, and a man’s crooked or upright conduct shows what he is.

Proverbs 21:9–19 — Justice and the Cry of the Poor

Two sayings about a contentious woman bracket the section, picturing a home so full of strife that a corner of the housetop or the wilderness would be easier to live in, a warning that applies to husbands as well as wives. Between them, the punished scoffer becomes a lesson to the simple, the man who shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will one day cry and not be heard, and doing justice is a joy to the just while destruction awaits the workers of iniquity.

Proverbs 21:20–29 — The Righteous Give and Do Not Spare

The wise keep the treasure and oil that a foolish man squanders, and whoever pursues righteousness and mercy finds life and honor along with the righteousness he sought. A wise man brings down the stronghold the mighty trusted in, a guarded tongue keeps the soul from troubles, the proud man earns the name “Scoffer,” and the lazy man craves all day while the righteous man gives without holding back.

Proverbs 21:30–31 — Deliverance Is of the LORD

No wisdom, understanding, or counsel can stand against the LORD. The horse is rightly made ready for battle, yet the victory comes from Him, so preparation is carried out in trust and never in place of it.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 21 gives God’s people reason to trust Him above every ruler. If the king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand, no throne is beyond His reach, a confidence that fuels prayer for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) instead of excusing their injustice. The closing verse keeps the same balance in war: the horse is still prepared, but trust rests on the LORD (compare Psalm 20:7).

The chapter also measures worship by the life behind it. The LORD does not set sacrifice aside, yet righteousness and justice please Him more (21:3), and an offering brought “with wicked intent” is an abomination all the more (21:27). It notices as well the man whose neighbor “finds no favor in his eyes” and the one who shuts his ears to the poor (21:10, 13); that warning targets a hard heart, not every unanswered prayer.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The LORD over rulers and plans. The king’s heart, every human counsel, and the outcome of battle are in His hand (21:1, 30–31).

Justice above ritual. Righteousness and justice please the LORD more than sacrifice, the wicked who refuse justice are destroyed, and doing justice is a joy to the just (21:3, 7, 15, 27).

Pride and the scoffer. A haughty look and a proud heart are sin, the proud and haughty man is called a scoffer, and the scoffer’s punishment teaches the simple (21:4, 11, 24).

Wealth gained and wasted. Diligent plans lead to plenty, while haste, lies, love of pleasure, and the fool’s squandering end in loss (21:5–6, 17, 20).

The poor and the generous. The ear shut to the poor brings an unheard cry, and the lazy man craves all day while the righteous man gives freely (21:13, 25–26).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Rivers of water (21:1). Most likely the irrigation channels a farmer directs where he wants the water to go. The picture shows how readily the LORD directs a ruler, as when He “stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” (Ezra 1:1).

Contentious woman (21:9, 19). A wife given to quarreling, and in 21:19 to anger as well. The sayings portray the misery of strife in a home, not a joke about wives; 21:9 returns almost word for word in 25:24.

Scoffer (21:11, 24). The scorner who will not be taught, whose problem lies in the will rather than the mind. Proverbs 21:24 shows where his contempt for correction comes from: the proud and haughty man “acts with arrogant pride.”

Ransom (21:18). A price paid to set someone free. The saying most likely means that the trouble the wicked plan for the righteous falls on themselves instead (compare 11:8), though its exact sense is debated. In the gospel God reverses that order in grace, for Christ suffered “the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).

Abomination (21:27). Something the LORD finds detestable. Here even a sacrifice becomes one when a wicked heart offers it, and it is all the more detestable when brought with wicked intent (compare 15:8).

sections.title: Justice and the Cry of the Poor
The Righteous Give and Do Not Spare

1.brief: In the LORD’s hand the king’s heart is turned wherever He wishes, the way a farmer guides water through irrigation channels. Even the mightiest ruler is under God’s direction, which gives His people reason to trust Him above every throne.
1.explain:
“The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD,”

Solomon begins with the most powerful man in his world. A king’s heart was where wars were declared, taxes set, and justice given or denied for a whole nation. In Proverbs the “heart” is the inner person, the place of thought, will, and desire, and this saying places that center of royal decision “in the hand of the LORD.” The hand pictures control and keeping. No throne is so high that it stands outside God’s reach, and Solomon, himself a king, writes as one whose own heart answered to Someone greater.

“Like the rivers of water;”

The “rivers of water” here are most naturally the channels a farmer cut to carry water across his fields. In a dry land water was guided through small ditches, and with a few strokes of a hoe a farmer could open one channel and close another. The water flows freely and follows its own nature, yet it goes where the farmer sends it. That is the force of the picture. It does not explain everything about how God’s rule and a king’s choices fit together, but it shows both at work: the king really decides, and God really directs, without a struggle and without destroying the king’s own will.

“He turns it wherever He wishes.”

The LORD is the one who turns, and He turns the king’s heart “wherever He wishes.” Scripture shows Him doing this with rulers who did not know Him, as when “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” to send the exiles home (Ezra 1:1). The saying does not excuse a ruler’s injustice, and it gives no reason to stop praying for those in authority. It is the reason such prayer makes sense (1 Timothy 2:1–2). God’s people can trust Him above every throne, because He governs the hearts of those who sit on them.
1.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “rivers” in “rivers of water” is the one used in Psalm 1:3 of the tree “Planted by the rivers of water” (Psalm 1:3). It means a channel or stream, often a channel cut for irrigation, rather than a great river. That is why the ESV and NLT render it “stream.”

The chapter opens and closes with the LORD’s rule over the two great powers of Solomon’s world, the throne (21:1) and the army (21:30–31).

2.brief: Every person thinks his own way is right, but the LORD weighs the heart. Self-approval proves nothing, since God looks beneath the choices to the motives that drive them.
2.explain:
“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes,”

The saying widens from the king to every person. A man’s “way” is his course of conduct, the choices and habits that make up a life. “Right in his own eyes” describes self-assessment: from the inside, our own path almost always looks straight and justified. Israel’s darkest period is summed up in the same words: “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). People are rarely the villains of their own stories. We explain, excuse, and approve ourselves almost by instinct, which is why our own verdict cannot settle the matter.

“But the LORD weighs the hearts.”

Against that self-approval stands the LORD who “weighs.” The picture comes from the marketplace scale, where goods were tested against honest weights. God does not stop at the visible path; He measures the heart, the motives and desires that drive the choices. Two people can do the same thing for very different reasons, and God weighs the difference. The line humbles the person who is sure of himself, and it also gives every reader somewhere to go. The One who measures the heart accurately is the One who can correct what He finds.
2.notes:
The verse nearly repeats 16:2, “All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, But the LORD weighs the spirits” (16:2). Such repetitions with small changes of wording are common in Solomon’s collection.

The same description of God, “He who weighs the hearts” (24:12), returns in the words of the wise, where it warns against pleading ignorance.

3.brief: Doing what is right and just pleases the LORD more than offering sacrifice. Worship is not set aside, but worship cut off from obedience cannot take the place of a righteous life (compare 1 Samuel 15:22).
3.explain:
“To do righteousness and justice”

“Righteousness” is right living measured by God’s standard, and “justice” is fair dealing, giving others what is due to them in court, in business, and in daily life. Together the two words describe a whole way of life toward God and neighbor. They name what the LORD chose Abraham’s family to practice, “that they keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice” (Genesis 18:19). The weight falls on the verb “to do.” The verse is about righteousness practiced, not merely admired.

“Is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.”

Sacrifice was commanded by God and stood at the center of Israel’s worship, so the comparison is striking. It is more striking from Solomon, who at the temple’s dedication offered sheep and oxen “that could not be counted or numbered for multitude” (1 Kings 8:5). The saying does not cancel worship; it ranks it. An offering cannot stand in for a just life or cover a settled pattern of injustice. Samuel told Saul, “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22), and the prophets said the same (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:8). Coming right after 21:2, the saying follows naturally from it. The God who weighs hearts is not satisfied with ritual that leaves the heart and the life unchanged.
3.notes: Sacrifice appears near the beginning and the end of the chapter. Here righteousness and justice please the LORD more than sacrifice, and in 21:27 the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination.

4.brief: Haughty eyes, a proud heart, and even the plowing of the wicked are all sin. When pride sits at the center of a life, even ordinary work done from that heart is tainted by it.
4.explain:
“A haughty look, a proud heart,”

The verse names pride twice, once on the face and once within. In Hebrew, “a haughty look” is literally height of eyes, the raised eyes of someone who looks down on others. “A proud heart” is the source of that look, a heart swollen with its own importance. The look shows the heart, and the heart produces the look. “A proud look” heads the list of things the LORD hates (6:17). Proverbs treats pride as a matter of the heart that the fear of the LORD exposes, because a right view of God leaves no room for an inflated view of self.

“And the plowing of the wicked are sin.”

The third item is unexpected. The “plowing of the wicked” is his ordinary work, the field he cultivates to make a living. Plowing is not wrong in itself, yet when it comes from a proud and godless heart, even everyday labor is counted as sin, because it is done without reference to God and for self alone. The verse names a look and a heart before any outward deed and calls all of it “sin.” Pride does not have to do anything dramatic to be evil in God’s sight. It colors everything a person does, including the work that looks perfectly normal.
4.notes: The Hebrew word rendered “plowing” can also be read as “lamp,” and the ESV and the NASB (1995) translate it that way. On that reading the line speaks of the outward prosperity of the wicked, since a burning lamp pictures life and well-being in Proverbs (13:9). The KJV, like the NKJV, has “plowing,” with “light” in its margin.

5.brief: The careful plans of the diligent lead to plenty, but everyone who rushes ahead in haste comes to poverty. Patient, thoughtful work builds over time, while impatience cuts corners and loses what it grasps for.
5.explain:
“The plans of the diligent lead surely to plenty,”

The diligent person in Proverbs is the steady, careful worker, the counterpart of the lazy man. Here the emphasis falls on his “plans,” his forethought. Diligence joins thinking to steady effort. He considers what needs doing, and then he keeps at it. Such plans “lead surely to plenty,” which describes the normal direction careful work moves in. Like the book’s other sayings about wealth, this states how God’s world generally works. It does not promise that every diligent person will become rich.

“But those of everyone who is hasty, surely to poverty.”

The contrast is not the one we expect. Proverbs usually sets the diligent against the lazy (10:4), but here the opposite is “everyone who is hasty.” The hasty person may be busy and may work hard, but he rushes ahead without thinking, grabs at quick returns, and cuts corners. The repeated “surely” shows how dependable both outcomes are. Hurry can empty a life as surely as idleness, and elsewhere the book warns that “he who hastens to be rich will not go unpunished” (28:20). The skill taught here is patience joined to planning.

6.brief: Treasure gained by a lying tongue is a vapor that vanishes, the chasing of those who are really seeking death. Wealth won through deceit does not last, and the pursuit of it leads toward ruin.
6.explain:
“Getting treasures by a lying tongue”

The verse looks at wealth gained through deceit: false claims, misleading promises, dishonest contracts. “Treasures” suggests more than a living; it is wealth stored up. The “lying tongue” is one of the things the LORD hates (6:17), and here it becomes a method of getting rich.

“Is the fleeting fantasy”

A “fleeting fantasy” has no substance and is quickly gone, like a breath of vapor on a cold morning that the wind carries off. Dishonest gain looks solid while it is being counted. It has no lasting foundation, and it vanishes.

“of those who seek death.”

The final phrase exposes the irony. The liar thinks he is pursuing treasure, but the verse counts him among “those who seek death.” He does not intend to die, yet the method he has chosen moves him toward ruin. Proverbs often describes sin as a road whose end is hidden from the one walking it, and this saying names the end plainly. The chapter returns to roads that end in death at 21:16 and 21:25.
6.notes:
Behind “fleeting fantasy” stand two Hebrew words. The first means vapor or breath and is the word Ecclesiastes uses for “vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). The second means driven away, so the picture is a breath of vapor blown off by the wind.

The ESV closes the verse with a snare of death instead of seekers of death. The ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) and the Latin Vulgate read “snares of death,” and some Hebrew manuscripts have the Hebrew word for “snares,” which differs by one letter from the word for “those who seek.” Most Hebrew manuscripts, followed by the NKJV and KJV, read “those who seek death.”

7.brief: Violence carried out by the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The harm they plan for others turns back on them, and their own refusal of justice is the cause.
7.explain:
“The violence of the wicked will destroy them,”

“Violence” covers robbery, oppression, and every kind of harm done by force to gain an advantage over others. The wicked use violence as a tool, but the verse says it “will destroy them.” The Hebrew verb behind “destroy” means to drag or sweep away, so the picture is of the wicked being hauled off like a catch in a net. The harm they plan for others turns back and carries them off. Proverbs said the same of the violent gang in its first chapter: “they lie in wait for their own blood” (1:18).

“Because they refuse to do justice.”

The second line gives the reason. The wicked are not ignorant of what is right; they “refuse to do justice.” Their ruin is the outcome of a settled choice rather than an accident. The Hebrew verb translated “refuse” returns at 21:25, where the lazy man’s hands “refuse to labor.” In both sayings the trouble lies in the will. The verse is the reverse side of 21:3. The LORD prizes doing justice above sacrifice, and those who refuse to do it bring destruction on themselves.
7.notes: The ESV and NLT render the verb “sweep” and “sweeps,” closer to the picture in the Hebrew than the NKJV’s “destroy.”

8.brief: Crooked is the way of the guilty man, but the conduct of the pure is upright. What a person is inside shows in how he lives, whether twisted or straight.
8.explain:
“The way of a guilty man is perverse;”

A man’s “way” is his conduct, the course of his life. The guilty man’s way is “perverse,” twisted and crooked, full of turns and evasions. Guilt does not produce straight living. It produces concealment, and one cover-up leads to another. A person with something to hide cannot walk in a straight line, because he must keep adjusting his story and his path.

“But as for the pure, his work is right.”

The “pure” person is clean in heart and conduct before God. His “work,” what he does day by day, “is right,” straight and upright. The line is plain and undramatic, and that fits its meaning, since purity shows itself in ordinary honest work. The saying answers 21:2. There a man’s way is “right in his own eyes”; here the pure man’s work actually is right. The outward life reveals the inner condition, twisted or straight, and the God who weighs the heart sees both.
8.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “guilty” occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its meaning has been debated. The KJV rendered the line with “froward” and “strange,” while modern versions agree with the NKJV’s “guilty.”

The word “right” in 21:8 is the same Hebrew word as in 21:2, so the contrast between seeming right and being right is verbal as well as conceptual.

9.brief: It is better to live cramped in a corner of the rooftop than to share a whole house with a quarrelsome wife. The proverb pictures how strife in a home can make a spacious house unbearable, a warning that applies to husbands as well as wives.
9.explain:
“Better to dwell in a corner of a housetop,”

Houses in Israel had flat roofs used for work, storage, drying produce, and sleeping in hot weather. A “corner of a housetop” would be a cramped and exposed spot, open to sun, wind, and rain. This is a “better than” saying, and it names the lesser good first: a tiny, uncomfortable corner outside.

“Than in a house shared with a contentious woman.”

The alternative is a whole house, with all its room and comfort, shared with a “contentious woman,” a wife given to constant quarreling. The comparison shows that strife can make a spacious home unbearable. The worth of a home lies in its peace more than in its size. The saying speaks from a husband’s side because the book addresses a son, but it portrays strife in a home and is no joke about wives. Proverbs names the “contentious man” as well (26:21), and the warning applies to husbands as much as wives. Every member of a household either builds its peace or wears it down.
9.notes: The saying is repeated almost word for word in 25:24, and 21:19 restates it with a harsher picture. The two contentious-woman sayings, 21:9 and 21:19, open and close this section of the chapter.

10.brief: Evil is what the wicked person’s soul craves, and he shows no kindness even to his neighbor. His desires are so bent toward harm that those closest to him receive no mercy.
10.explain:
“The soul of the wicked desires evil;”

“Soul” here means the inner self with its appetites and longings. The wicked person does not simply fall into evil now and then. He craves it. His desires have been bent until harm itself is what he wants. Proverbs often traces conduct back to desire, and this verse goes to the root: what a person longs for determines how he lives.

“His neighbor finds no favor in his eyes.”

The result shows up close to home. The “neighbor” is the person who lives beside him, someone he deals with every day. Even this person “finds no favor in his eyes”; he receives no kindness, pity, or grace. A heart that hungers for evil cannot spare mercy even for the man next door. The saying stands in a section about justice and the poor, and it describes the kind of heart that shuts out the needs of others, the same hardness 21:13 goes on to warn against. Wickedness begins as an appetite and shows itself as hardness toward the people nearest at hand.

11.brief: When the scoffer is punished, the simple learn wisdom by watching; when the wise is taught, he gains knowledge directly. The scoffer’s punishment serves as a lesson to others, while the wise person learns from instruction itself (compare 19:25).
11.explain:
“When the scoffer is punished, the simple is made wise;”

The scoffer is the proud mocker who will not accept correction (9:7–8; 13:1). His problem lies in the will: he will not be wise. When he is punished he may learn nothing, but someone else does. The “simple” person, uncommitted and easily led, watches what happens and gains wisdom from it. Judgment on one man teaches others. The simple stands at a crossroads, and the scoffer’s punishment can turn him toward the right path.

“But when the wise is instructed, he receives knowledge.”

The wise person learns another way. He needs no painful example. When he “is instructed,” he “receives knowledge” directly. The verse sets three people side by side by how they learn. The scoffer may not learn even from his own punishment, the simple learns by watching, and the wise learns from a word. The same order appears in 19:25. The better course is to be the kind of person who can be taught by instruction and does not need hard lessons to see what is true.
11.notes:
Proverbs 19:25 makes the same point with different wording: “Strike a scoffer, and the simple will become wary” (19:25).

The Hebrew verb behind “instructed” in 21:11 is the same verb translated “wisely considers” in 21:12, and “understanding” in 21:16 is a form of that verb used as a noun. The verb has to do with insight, so the repeated word links these sayings: the wise gain insight when instructed, the Righteous One considers the house of the wicked with full insight, and the wanderer leaves the way of insight.

12.brief: God in His righteousness takes careful notice of the house of the wicked and overthrows the wicked for their evil. He is not unaware of what goes on in their homes, and His judgment falls in its time.
12.explain:
“The righteous God wisely considers the house of the wicked,”

The NKJV identifies the subject as “The righteous God,” the Righteous One who sees all. He “wisely considers” the house of the wicked, looking carefully and with full understanding at what goes on inside it. The “house” is both the dwelling and the household, the family and fortune the wicked man has built. It may look secure and prosperous from the street, but nothing in it escapes God’s notice.

“Overthrowing the wicked for their wickedness.”

God’s careful consideration leads to action. He overthrows the wicked “for their wickedness,” so the judgment matches the guilt. He is never hasty or careless in judgment; He considers before He overthrows. Believers troubled by the apparent success of the wicked can rest in this. The house is being weighed even while it seems to stand firm. The verse does not say when the overthrow comes. It says that the Righteous One sees, and that His judgment is just.
12.notes: The Hebrew has no separate word for “God” in the first line. It uses “righteous” as a title, the Righteous One, and the NKJV supplies “God” to make the subject clear. The KJV instead reads the first line of a righteous man who considers the house of the wicked, and supplies God as the subject of the second line. The NKJV reading fits the second line, since overthrowing the wicked is God’s work.

13.brief: Whoever closes his ears to the cry of the poor will one day cry out himself and not be heard. Hardness toward the needy closes a person off from the mercy he will someday need; the warning targets a hard heart, not every unanswered prayer.
13.explain:
“Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor”

To shut one’s ears is a deliberate act. The man hears the cry and chooses not to listen. The “cry of the poor” is the call for help from those without money or power, often in the face of injustice. The picture is of a settled habit, a hardened refusal of mercy. God’s own character stands behind the warning. He is the God who hears the poor, and of the poor man who cries to Him He said, “I will hear, for I am gracious” (Exodus 22:27).

“Will also cry himself and not be heard.”

The positions reverse. The man who would not listen becomes the one crying out, and now no one hears him. The ones who do not hear him may be other people who remember his hardness, or it may be God, whose mercy he refused to imitate. James states the principle: “judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13). The verse warns against a hard heart. It does not turn every unanswered prayer into punishment for neglecting the poor. What it does say clearly is that no one can expect mercy while refusing to show it.

14.brief: A secret gift calms anger, and a bribe slipped under the cloak quiets fierce wrath. The proverb observes how hidden payments work to buy peace, without approving bribery, which Proverbs condemns when it perverts justice (17:23).
14.explain:
“A gift in secret pacifies anger,”

The verse observes how life works. A gift given quietly calms someone’s anger. An angry person often cannot back down in public without losing face, and a private gift lets him lay his anger aside. Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau for this reason, saying, “I will appease him with the present that goes before me” (Genesis 32:20). A quiet gift can be a wise way to make peace.

“And a bribe behind the back, strong wrath.”

The second line moves into darker territory. A “bribe behind the back,” hidden in the fold of a garment, quiets even “strong wrath.” The saying states a fact of life: hidden payments buy peace and influence. It does not approve the practice. The same expression appears where “A wicked man accepts a bribe behind the back To pervert the ways of justice” (17:23). Whether a gift is wise or wicked depends on its purpose. A gift that restores peace without twisting justice can be right, while a bribe that buys a verdict or excuses wrongdoing is condemned. Placed in a section about justice and the poor, the observation also shows how easily the powerful can be bought.
14.notes: “Behind the back” renders a Hebrew word for the bosom, the fold of the robe where something could be carried out of sight. The NASB and KJV translate it “bosom.”

15.brief: Doing justice is a joy to the just, but it brings terror to those who practice evil. The same act of justice that gladdens the righteous is ruin to the wicked.
15.explain:
“It is a joy for the just to do justice,”

For the just person, doing right is not a burden carried reluctantly. It is a “joy.” Such joy shows what God does in a heart. The just person takes pleasure in fair dealing, in giving people their due, and in setting wrong things right. The line also includes justice carried out in the courts, which gladdens the righteous because it protects them and vindicates what is good.

“But destruction will come to the workers of iniquity.”

The same justice that gladdens the just brings “destruction” to those who practice evil. The Hebrew word translated “destruction” usually means ruin, and many translations render it “terror” here, the dismay of evildoers when justice arrives. Justice does not change; what changes is a person’s relation to it. For the righteous, the arrival of justice is good news. For the “workers of iniquity,” those who make a practice of wrongdoing, it means exposure and ruin.
15.notes:
The Hebrew of the first line can be read as the just person’s own delight in doing justice, as in the NKJV, or as a statement about what happens when justice is done in the land. The ESV takes the second view, with “joy” for the righteous and “terror” for evildoers.

The second line is identical in the NKJV to the second line of 10:29, “But destruction will come to the workers of iniquity” (10:29).

16.brief: Wandering off the way of understanding brings a person to rest in the company of the dead. Drifting from wisdom is not harmless; it ends in death.
16.explain:
“A man who wanders from the way of understanding”

The “way of understanding” is the path of wisdom the whole book sets out. This man “wanders” from it. He does not necessarily set out to rebel. He drifts, steps off the path, and then takes another step. The danger Proverbs keeps naming is drift, the gradual turning away of someone who never committed himself to wisdom: “the turning away of the simple will slay them” (1:32).

“Will rest in the assembly of the dead.”

The irony lies in the word “rest.” The wanderer finds rest at last, but it is the rest of the dead. The “assembly of the dead” is the company of those who have gone down to the grave. He joins a congregation, but it is the wrong one. Proverbs used the same picture for the guests of Folly: “the dead are there” (9:18). Wandering from wisdom is never neutral, because every path ends somewhere. The warning is given so that the wanderer can turn back while he still can.
16.notes: The Hebrew word for “the dead” here is the one used in 2:18 and 9:18, which the NKJV also renders “the dead.” It refers to the departed in the realm of the dead.

17.brief: Whoever loves pleasure will end up poor, and the one who loves wine and oil will not grow rich. Living for luxury and good times drains the resources it enjoys.
17.explain:
“He who loves pleasure will be a poor man;”

The key word is “loves.” Pleasure in itself is not condemned, since God gives good things to enjoy. The problem is a person whose life is organized around enjoyment, who spends whatever he has on the next good time. Such a person “will be a poor man,” because living for pleasure consumes the resources that pay for it.

“He who loves wine and oil will not be rich.”

“Wine and oil” were the luxuries of a feast. Wine was served at celebrations, and fragrant oil was used to anoint the head and skin at banquets. Scripture counts both among God’s gifts: “wine that makes glad the heart of man, Oil to make his face shine” (Psalm 104:15). The man who loves them, who makes feasting his aim, “will not be rich.” The verse does not say that every poor person loves pleasure, and it does not forbid enjoying God’s gifts. It warns that loving the gift more than the Giver drains both the purse and the life. The oil returns in 21:20, stored in the dwelling of the wise.
17.notes: The word translated “pleasure” is the same Hebrew word translated “joy” in 21:15. The just find joy in doing justice, while the man who loves joy for its own sake ends poor.

18.brief: The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the unfaithful for the upright, as the trouble the wicked plan for the godly falls on themselves instead (compare 11:8). In Christ, God reverses this order in grace, for He suffered “the just for the unjust” (1 Peter 3:18).
18.explain:
“The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous,”

A “ransom” is a price paid to set someone free or to take someone’s place. Here the wicked themselves become the ransom. The most likely meaning is that the trouble the wicked plan for the righteous falls on the wicked instead, and the righteous are delivered. Proverbs has already said, “The righteous is delivered from trouble, And it comes to the wicked instead” (11:8). Scripture gives examples, as when “they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 7:10). The exact sense of “ransom” in this saying is debated, but the reversal is clear.

“And the unfaithful for the upright.”

The second line repeats the thought in new words. The “unfaithful” are the treacherous, people who betray trust, and the “upright” are those who walk straight. Under God’s justice, treachery does not have the last word. This describes how God generally governs His world. The righteous still suffer in this age, and Proverbs does not promise otherwise.

Proverbs itself does not go further, but the gospel shows God reversing this order in grace. At the cross the Righteous One took the place of the unrighteous: “Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The proverb shows God’s justice falling on the wicked; the cross shows His mercy providing a substitute for them.
18.notes: “Ransom” translates the Hebrew word for a payment given to redeem or cover a life, as in Exodus 21:30. Isaiah uses it of nations given in Israel’s place: “I gave Egypt for your ransom” (Isaiah 43:3).

19.brief: It is better to live alone in the wilderness than with a quarrelsome and angry wife. Repeating the thought of verse 9 with even starker imagery, the saying closes the section with the misery of a home filled with constant strife.
19.explain:
“Better to dwell in the wilderness,”

The saying repeats the thought of 21:9 with a starker picture. There the cramped corner of a roof was better. Here it is the “wilderness,” the dry and empty land beyond the towns, where life was hard and lonely. Living alone in the desert would be easier than the alternative.

“Than with a contentious and angry woman.”

The new element is anger. The woman is not only “contentious,” given to quarreling, but also “angry,” irritable and provoking. Quarreling joined to anger can make a home lonelier than the desert. Two such sayings in one chapter show how seriously Proverbs weighs the atmosphere of a home. As in 21:9, the saying portrays strife in a household and applies to husbands as well as wives. It warns about what constant anger does to a home; it is not counsel to abandon a marriage. With this saying the section closes as it began.

20.brief: Precious treasure and oil are stored in the house of the wise, but a foolish man devours everything he has. Wisdom saves and provides, while folly spends whatever comes to hand.
20.explain:
“There is desirable treasure,”

The verse describes the house of the wise. “Desirable treasure” means valuable goods, things worth having and worth keeping.

“And oil in the dwelling of the wise,”

Oil was a basic store in an Israelite household, used for cooking, for lamps, and for anointing, and a full supply meant the family was ready for what lay ahead. In the “dwelling of the wise” there are reserves. Wisdom provides and saves. It does not spend everything the moment it arrives, so the household has something for tomorrow and something to share.

“But a foolish man squanders it.”

The fool squanders what he has. The Hebrew pictures swallowing or devouring: whatever comes in goes straight down. He may have the same income as the wise man, yet it never stays. What separates the two houses is what is done with what comes in. Read with the rest of the chapter, treasure gained by lies vanishes (21:6) and the lover of oil ends poor (21:17), while treasure honestly gained and wisely kept remains. The verse teaches stewardship rather than hoarding, for the righteous are also those who give freely (21:26).

21.brief: Whoever pursues righteousness and faithful love finds life, righteousness, and honor. The one who seeks right living and kindness receives far more than he sought, including the very righteousness he pursued.
21.explain:
“He who follows righteousness and mercy”

The Hebrew verb behind “follows” means to pursue, to chase after something with purpose. The person described makes “righteousness and mercy” his aim. Righteousness is right living by God’s standard. “Mercy” is faithful, loyal love, the kindness that keeps its commitments. The two belong together. Righteousness without mercy grows hard, and mercy without righteousness grows soft. The one who pursues both reflects the character of God, who is both righteous and merciful.

“Finds life, righteousness, and honor.”

He finds more than he went after. He sought righteousness and mercy, and he “Finds life, righteousness, and honor.” Righteousness appears in both lines, so the one who pursues it finds it, and life and honor come with it. Solomon’s own story fits the pattern. He asked for wisdom, and God said, “I have also given you what you have not asked: both riches and honor” (1 Kings 3:13). Like the book’s other sayings about reward, this describes what God delights to give and how His world generally works. It is not a formula that guarantees honor in this life to everyone who does right.
21.notes:
“Mercy” translates the Hebrew word for steadfast, loyal love, the word often used of God’s faithful love for His people.

In the second line, the Hebrew word translated “righteousness” can also mean vindication or well-being: being shown to be in the right and enjoying the blessing that follows. Some translations take it that way and render it “prosperity.” The NKJV, ESV, NASB, and NLT repeat “righteousness.”

22.brief: A wise man can climb the walls of a city held by mighty men and bring down the stronghold they trusted in. Wisdom accomplishes what force alone cannot, prevailing over strength and fortifications.
22.explain:
“A wise man scales the city of the mighty,”

The picture is military. A “city of the mighty” is a fortified town defended by strong warriors. A wise man “scales” it, climbing its walls and taking it. Strength and high walls seemed to make the city safe, yet wisdom found a way in.

“And brings down the trusted stronghold.”

The “trusted stronghold” is the fortress in which the defenders placed their confidence, and the wise man brings it down. Wisdom accomplishes what force alone cannot. Insight, strategy, and good counsel can overcome superior numbers and thick walls. Ecclesiastes tells of “a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city” (Ecclesiastes 9:15). The saying also exposes what the mighty trusted. Their confidence rested on walls, and walls were not enough. The chapter returns to the theme at its close, where neither counsel nor the war horse can stand in for the LORD (21:30–31).
22.notes: “Trusted stronghold” renders a Hebrew phrase meaning literally the strength in which it trusted, which puts the stress on the defenders’ confidence.

23.brief: Whoever guards his mouth and tongue keeps himself out of trouble. Much of the distress people suffer comes from careless words, so watching one’s speech protects one’s life.
23.explain:
“Whoever guards his mouth and tongue”

To “guard” is to keep watch, as a sentry watches a gate. The “mouth and tongue” together cover what a person says and how he says it. Guarding them means thinking before speaking, holding back angry or careless words, and refusing gossip and lies.

“Keeps his soul from troubles.”

The one who guards his mouth “Keeps his soul,” that is, protects his life, “from troubles.” Many of the troubles people suffer walk in through their own mouths: a quarrel started by a sharp word, trust broken by gossip, a rash promise that cannot be kept. The book has said this before: “He who guards his mouth preserves his life” (13:3). Not every trouble comes from words, and the verse does not claim that it does. But careless speech brings a great deal of trouble that could have been avoided, and a guarded tongue spares a person much grief.
23.notes: In Hebrew the same verb stands behind “guards” and “keeps,” so the guard set over the mouth becomes a guard over the life.

24.brief: The proud and haughty person has earned the name Scoffer, because he acts with arrogant pride. Contempt for correction grows out of pride, and the scoffer’s name tells what he has become.
24.explain:
“A proud and haughty man—”

The verse describes a man marked by pride and arrogance. “Proud” and “haughty” together stress inflated self-importance and contempt for others. This is the proud heart of 21:4, now grown into a whole character.

“Scoffer” is his name;

In Scripture a name often describes a nature, and this man has earned the name “Scoffer.” The scoffer is the most hardened figure in the book’s gallery of fools. He mocks correction and will not be taught (9:7–8; 13:1); his problem is not that he cannot be wise but that he will not. This verse shows where the scoffing comes from. Contempt for correction grows out of pride. The proud man cannot accept rebuke, because rebuke means he was wrong, so he scorns the one who gives it.

“He acts with arrogant pride.”

His actions match his name. He “acts with arrogant pride,” an insolence that overflows into how he treats others. Pride does not stay hidden in the heart. Practiced long enough, it becomes who a person is, and others begin to name him by it. The book sets the alternative beside this portrait, for the LORD “scorns the scornful, But gives grace to the humble” (3:34).

25.brief: Desire kills the lazy man, because his hands refuse to work. He wants things badly but will not labor for them, and that unsatisfied craving destroys him.
25.explain:
“The desire of the lazy man kills him,”

The lazy man is not empty of desire. He is full of it. He wants comfort, food, and success, but his wanting never turns into work. The verse says his “desire” kills him. Unsatisfied craving eats away at him, and the want it leaves behind can bring real ruin. Proverbs describes the same man elsewhere: “The soul of a lazy man desires, and has nothing” (13:4).

“For his hands refuse to labor.”

The reason lies in his hands. They are able, but they “refuse.” In Hebrew it is the same verb used of the wicked who “refuse to do justice” (21:7). Laziness, like injustice, is a choice of the will, which is why Proverbs speaks so sharply about it. The verse is not describing someone who cannot work because of illness, disability, or lack of opportunity; Proverbs distinguishes laziness from inability and genuine need. It describes a man who could work and will not, who wants the fruit of labor without the labor.

26.brief: All day long he craves more and more, but the righteous gives without holding back. Set beside verse 25, the saying contrasts the lazy man who only wants with the righteous person who works and is free to give.
26.explain:
“He covets greedily all day long,”

Following 21:25, the most natural subject is the lazy man. All day long he craves. The line repeats the language of desire from the verse before, describing a man whose whole day is spent wanting. His life reaches inward, toward what he lacks and will not work for.

“But the righteous gives and does not spare.”

Against him stands the righteous person, whose life reaches outward. He “gives and does not spare,” giving without holding back. The contrast is between craving and generosity, and it has nothing to do with being rich or poor. The righteous person works and so has something to give, while the lazy man only wants. Paul joins work and giving the same way: “let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give him who has need” (Ephesians 4:28). Generosity is one of the clearest marks of righteousness in Proverbs, and this line gives the section its title.
26.notes:
In Hebrew the first line doubles the language of desire. The verb “covets” and the noun that follows it share the root of the word “desire” in 21:25, so the Hebrew behind “He covets greedily” says literally that he desires a desire. The repetition stresses how intense the craving is, as if he wants and keeps on wanting, and the shared word ties this saying to the lazy man of 21:25.

The NLT treats the first line as a general statement about greedy people rather than a continuation of the lazy man of 21:25. The NKJV, ESV, and NASB (1995) keep the singular “he,” which most naturally refers back to him.

27.brief: The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD, and even more so when he brings it with an evil purpose. Religious offerings from a heart set on wrongdoing are worse than empty; they offend God, recalling verse 3.
27.explain:
“The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination;”

An “abomination” is something the LORD finds detestable. A sacrifice was meant to be an act of worship, but when a wicked person brings it while holding on to his wickedness, it becomes offensive to God. This line repeats the first line of 15:8, which adds that “the prayer of the upright is His delight” (15:8). God takes no pleasure in outward religion from a heart that refuses Him. The saying answers 21:3 near the start of the chapter.

“How much more when he brings it with wicked intent!”

The second line goes further. Some people not only bring offerings while living wickedly; they use the offering to cover or advance their wickedness. They bring it “with wicked intent,” as part of a deliberate evil plan. Absalom asked David, “let me go to Hebron and pay the vow which I made to the LORD” (2 Samuel 15:7), and used that occasion to launch his rebellion. Religion used as a disguise is doubly detestable, because it adds hypocrisy to sin and tries to make God an accomplice. The LORD who weighs the hearts sees the intent behind every offering (21:2).

28.brief: A false witness will perish, and his testimony with him. The second line is harder: the NKJV says the man who hears him “will speak endlessly,” which most likely means that the one who truly listens gives testimony that endures, while the liar is silenced.
28.explain:
“A false witness shall perish,”

A “false witness” lies in court, testifying to what he did not see or hear. In Israel such testimony could ruin a neighbor or even cost him his life, and the law required that the false witness receive the penalty he intended for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:18–19). The false witness “shall perish.” He will be exposed and cut off, and his testimony will come to nothing.

“But the man who hears him will speak endlessly.”

The second line is harder. The NKJV says that “the man who hears him will speak endlessly.” The likely meaning is that the man who truly listens, the careful witness who reports only what he actually heard, gives testimony that endures. He can speak on, and his word stands, while the liar is silenced. The contrast is between a word that perishes and a word that lasts. Other readings of the line exist, but this one best fits its contrast with the first line.
28.notes:
The Hebrew has no object after “hears”; the NKJV supplies “him.” The final phrase means literally to perpetuity, which the NKJV renders “endlessly” and the KJV renders “speaketh constantly.”

Translations divide over the second line. The ESV and the NASB (1995) take it as the lasting word of a man who listens, close to the NKJV. Earlier editions of the NIV read it in the opposite direction, that whoever listens to the false witness will be “destroyed forever.” The current NIV (2011) instead has a “careful listener” who will “testify successfully,” and the NLT speaks of a credible witness being allowed to speak.

29.brief: The wicked man puts on a hard, bold face, but the upright person thinks through his way and makes it firm. Brazen confidence is set against careful, honest direction.
29.explain:
“A wicked man hardens his face,”

To harden the face is to put on a bold, brazen expression that shows no shame and does not soften when confronted. The wicked man bluffs his way through. He meets correction with defiance and wrongdoing with a straight face. The immoral woman of chapter 7 wears the same kind of face when she meets the young man “With an impudent face” (7:13). This firmness belongs to a conscience that has stopped listening.

“But as for the upright, he establishes his way.”

The upright person is firm too, in another way. He “establishes his way,” thinking through his course and setting it on solid ground. His confidence comes from integrity and careful thought, and it has no need of a hard face. Two kinds of firmness stand side by side. One refuses to be moved by truth, and the other is steady because it rests on truth. Determination is not a virtue in itself; what matters is what a person is determined about.
29.notes: The Hebrew text preserves two readings of the verb in the second line. The letters written in the text give “establishes,” which the NKJV follows. A note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to read a word that differs by one letter and means “understands” or “considers.” The ESV follows the margin reading, saying that the upright “gives thought” to his ways, and the KJV margin gives “considereth.” Either reading fits the contrast with the wicked man’s hard face.

30.brief: No wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel can stand against the LORD. Every human plan, however clever, is finally answerable to Him, and none can overturn His purpose.
30.explain:
“There is no wisdom or understanding”

Proverbs praises wisdom and understanding on nearly every page and urges the reader to seek them above silver and gold. Here the book sets them in their proper order. No wisdom and no understanding, however great, can stand against God. Human wisdom is His gift, “For the LORD gives wisdom” (2:6), and it cannot be turned successfully against its source.

“Or counsel against the LORD.”

“Counsel” is the plan or strategy that comes from consultation, the advice of skilled advisers. Kings depended on counselors, and Proverbs values them (11:14). Yet no counsel can prevail “against the LORD.” In David’s day Ahithophel’s advice was sound, but “the LORD had purposed to defeat the good advice of Ahithophel” (2 Samuel 17:14). Proverbs has already said that “the LORD’s counsel—that will stand” (19:21). This verse adds that nothing stands against it. Every human plan is finally answerable to Him, which is a warning to the proud planner and a comfort to all who trust the LORD.
30.notes: The three qualities named here resemble the ones Wisdom claims for herself in 8:14, “Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom; I am understanding” (8:14). The link is one of meaning rather than identical wording. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for “counsel,” but the words behind “wisdom” and “understanding” differ from those in 8:14. Here the book places such qualities beneath the LORD.

31.brief: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the LORD. Preparation is right and wise, yet the outcome rests in God’s hands, which is why trust must rest in Him and not in horses (compare Psalm 20:7).
31.explain:
“The horse is prepared for the day of battle,”

In Solomon’s day the horse was chiefly a weapon of war, pulling chariots and carrying horsemen, and Solomon himself “gathered chariots and horsemen” in great numbers (1 Kings 10:26). Preparing the horse for battle means doing what a responsible commander should do: training, equipping, and planning. The verse treats this as right. It does not tell anyone to leave the horse in the stable.

“But deliverance is of the LORD.”

“Deliverance” means rescue, victory, and salvation. However well the horse is prepared, the outcome of the battle belongs to God. Preparation is wise, but trust must rest in Him and not in the horse: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses; But we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). The verse closes the chapter where it began. The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand (21:1), no counsel stands against Him (21:30), and the battle is His. Diligence and trust are not rivals. The wise prepare fully and rely on God completely.
31.notes: The law of the king in Deuteronomy said that he “shall not multiply horses for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:16), which gives the saying added point in a collection associated with Israel’s kings.
